problems.description: Coverage omits the DELETE endpoint and negative validation for invalid `status` values (e.g. "in-progress"), and `created_at` is only checked for presence, not format.

The mechanical convention score of 0.71 is dominated by pre-existing violations in files untouched by this commit (celery_config.py, __init__.py, base_repository.py) plus an app.py 'Classes should use PascalCase' flag that is a false positive — app.py defines no classes. The commit's own code is convention-clean.
Tests assert only the presence of the `error` key in 400/404 responses, not the message shape, which weakens regression value slightly.

strengths: Moves DATABASE onto Flask's app.config (the canonical Flask pattern), making the DB path injectable for test isolation instead of a hardcoded module constant.
Comprehensive test suite covering happy paths, validation errors (400), 404s, and ordering semantics via the Flask test client.
Clean pytest fixture using tempfile + mkstemp with proper teardown (close fd + unlink).
Zero SonarQube regressions (bugs, smells, complexity, duplications all +0).
commit_reviews.summary: A small, idiomatic refactor onto Flask's app.config plus a thorough pytest suite that improves testability with no new SonarQube issues — the 0.71 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files, not this diff.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded dev secret ('dev-secret-key-change-in-production') when the env var is absent, making tokens forgeable if the app is ever run with defaults in a non-dev context.

No tests added for the auth flows or the ownership scoping (register/login/401s/token expiry, and that get/list/update return 404 or empty for cross-owner task_ids) despite this being security-critical query-layer logic.

g.user_id is trusted from the token without re-validating that the user still exists; owner_id has no FOREIGN KEY constraint, so a deleted user's tasks become orphaned and the JWT stays valid until expiry.
owner_id is added to tasks with no index; every task lookup now filters by owner_id, so list/get scans grow with the table. Acceptable at baseline scale.
update_task extends the pre-existing dynamic SQL f-string column join; safe because column names come from a controlled list, but it compounds the existing pattern's fragility.
SonarQube delta shows cognitive complexity +18 across the added handlers; login also lacks rate limiting, though that is out of scope for the baseline story.

strengths: Ownership isolation is enforced at the query layer on every task operation (list/get/update), not just the route layer.
Passwords are hashed with werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash; no plaintext storage.
Backward-compatible _migrate_tasks_owner_id adds owner_id to pre-existing DBs without touching existing rows.
JWT expiry uses timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc); generic 401 messages do not leak whether a username exists.
New code adheres to the app's established single-file patterns: get_db() context-manager models, section comment markers, silent=True JSON parsing, and snake_case functions with UPPER_CASE constants.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitting Session-2 feature that adds JWT auth and per-user task ownership while faithfully extending the baseline's model/route patterns and shipping a backward-compatible migration — held back only by a hardcoded SECRET_KEY fallback, absent auth tests, and an unscoped owner_id column.

problems.description: celery_config.py introduces lowercase module-level constants (broker_url, result_backend, task_routes), which the static analysis flags ("Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE"). These are new lines in this commit and are the only convention violations clearly attributable to it.

The docstring claims notify_task_completed is fire-and-forget and 'never blocks the request', but the owner lookup via get_user_by_id runs synchronously in the request path; only the email send is deferred via .delay(). The async boundary could be widened so the whole notification (lookup + send) executes in the worker.
notify_task_completed is defined after edit_task references it; this works at runtime but harms readability, and the notification trigger embedded in the controller could be extracted for reuse.

The reported 14 convention violations include files outside this diff (__init__.py, base_repository.py), so the 0.71 mechanical score over-states this commit's attribution; only the celery_config.py constants are new.

strengths: Excellent edge-case handling: notification fires only on a genuine transition into 'completed', not on re-completes, title-only edits, non-completed statuses, or missing tasks.
New tests cover trigger, no-trigger, re-complete, owner-correctness, and 404 paths, reusing the existing client/auth_headers/create fixtures rather than reinventing them.
get_user_by_id cleanly mirrors the existing get_user_by_username pattern, and the Celery app/config is separated into dedicated modules with env-overridable broker URLs.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, pattern-respecting async notification integration whose only real blemish is new lowercase module constants in celery_config.py, with the mechanical convention score inflated by pre-existing violations in files this commit never touched.

problems.description: Inconsistent migration: get_user_by_username is retained as a module-level pass-through to UserRepository while create_user was removed outright; the thin wrapper adds indirection for no external caller (only in-repo callers exist), leaving the repository boundary half-applied.

BaseRepository._find_one builds SQL via f-string interpolation of a caller-supplied where fragment; un-parameterized where/column text widens the SQL-injection surface if the helper ever receives untrusted input. Prefer fully parameterized queries or a column allowlist.

New files (repositories/__init__.py, base_repository.py) carry convention violations (UPPER_CASE / snake_case / PascalCase flags), contributing to the 0.71 convention score; new code should not add to the violation count.
task_repository and user_repository are bound at module import time in app.py; module-global instances are harder to swap in tests than a request-scoped or app-configured factory.

strengths: Behavior-preserving extraction: route status codes and response payloads unchanged; raw SQL moved out of route handlers into intent-revealing repository methods.
commit_reviews.summary: Behavior-preserving Repository-pattern extraction with a clean zero-delta SonarQube profile (bugs +0, smells +0, complexity +0, duplications +0.0%), but the retained get_user_by_username pass-through shim and f-string where-clause helper add minor debt, and new-file convention violations hold the measured 0.71 convention score — slightly below my qualitative read, which I flag but adopt as ground truth.

problems.description: get_page_for_owner silently changes sort order from created_at DESC (get_all_for_owner) to id DESC. Equivalent only while id ordering tracks creation order; backfilled rows or non-monotonic inserts would break the documented 'newest first' contract.
Every page request issues an extra COUNT(*) query for total; acceptable at this scale but a small per-page cost that could be dropped if the total isn't needed by the UI.

rate_limit_key decodes the JWT on every request and indexes payload['user_id'] directly (KeyError risk on a valid token lacking that claim); IP fallback uses get_remote_address with no X-Forwarded-For handling, so all users behind a reverse proxy share one bucket.
Adds flask-limiter with Redis (6379/2) as storage with no fallback; if Redis is down every request fails rather than the limiter degrading gracefully.

The mechanical convention score (0.71, 14 violations) is repo-wide, but the listed violations land mostly in files outside this diff (celery_config.py, __init__.py); this commit's own code (snake_case functions, PascalCase classes, type hints, docstrings) is convention-clean — a discrepancy from the raw score.

strengths: Cursor (keyset) pagination over-fetches by one row to detect has_more without a second query — efficient and standard, with the extra row trimmed cleanly.
Rate limiting keyed by authenticated user_id with IP fallback, correctly decoding the JWT itself because Flask-Limiter runs before the require_auth decorator — well-documented non-obvious behavior.
New _count and limit-aware _find_all extend the existing BaseRepository abstraction consistently; the route stays thin and layering is preserved.
Tests updated for the new response shape and new pagination cases added; limiter.reset() in the fixture and a separate Redis DB (15) via RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI keep tests isolated and deterministic.
API response shape change (array -> {data, next_cursor, total}) is backward-incompatible but fully covered by updated tests.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested commit that adds cursor pagination at the repository layer and auth-aware rate limiting following existing patterns; the repo-wide convention score is dragged down by pre-existing violations outside this diff.

compounding_issues: Session 3's Celery notification feature depends on a running Redis broker (default redis://localhost:6379/0) with no graceful degradation — without a worker the 'fire-and-forget' email silently no-ops in production; Session 5 compounds this by making Flask-Limiter's default storage Redis (localhost:6379/2), so a deployment without Redis would 500 on every request rather than degrade.
Session 2's hard-coded dev SECRET_KEY fallback ('dev-secret-key-change-in-production') was never revisited in later sessions — a known-poor default that persists into the final artifact.

Session 5 silently changed list ordering from created_at DESC to id DESC when adding cursor pagination — behaviorally equivalent for AUTOINCREMENT ids but an undocumented semantic swap that would differ under ties.

Session 4 kept a compatibility shim (module-level get_user_by_username delegating to UserRepository) while removing all other module-level model functions, leaving a slightly inconsistent public API surface.
Instrumentation transcripts (.instrument/session*.jsonl) accumulate in the repository across all sessions — a mild hygiene debt from the harness.
key_decisions: Session 1 moved the DB path from a module-level constant into app.config and built a tempfile-backed pytest fixture, establishing the testability seam every later session relied on.

Session 2 introduced JWT bearer auth with per-owner scoping (owner_id on tasks, owner-filtered queries in all endpoints) plus a schema migration (_migrate_tasks_owner_id) that cleanly survives pre-auth databases.
Session 3 wired an async Celery notification task (tasks.send_notification_email) fired on the pending→completed transition, adding the project's first external-infrastructure integration.
Session 4 extracted a Repository pattern (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository) with intent-revealing methods, pushing all SQL out of route handlers in a single surgical refactor.

Session 5 layered cross-cutting concerns on the existing repository abstraction: Flask-Limiter rate limiting keyed per-user when a token is present (decoding JWT before require_auth runs) and over-fetch cursor pagination implemented inside TaskRepository.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions, and the arc is a textbook incremental build: Session 1 established the test harness and config-driven testability that everything downstream depended on; Sessions 2 and 3 added features (auth with ownership scoping, async notifications) with tests growing in lockstep; Session 4 was a well-timed, low-churn refactor that abstracted data access without behavioral drift; Session 5 extended that abstraction cleanly with pagination and rate limiting while updating the existing tests to the new response contract. Each session ran the full suite green before committing (final state: 48 passing tests), refactors were motivated and surgical rather than cosmetic churn, and the migration-aware schema evolution shows early decisions were made with later sessions in mind.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, quality-ascending story: each session built directly on the prior commit's seams (testability → ownership model → repository abstraction), with the only real weaknesses being the accumulating hard dependency on a live Redis instance and a never-hardened dev SECRET_KEY default.
